What makes a request coercive is a specific pattern: no indication that citations were actually lacking, no suggestion of which body of work to consult, and a directive to cite only the editor's own journal, a combination documented by Wilhite and Fong's 2012 survey, in which about one in five academics reported experiencing it and 86% considered it unethical.

question: According to COPE's guidance for editors, why might the same degree of text recycling be judged differently depending on where in a paper it appears?
option_a: COPE treats all sections of a paper as functionally identical when assessing recycled text
option_b: Only recycled text appearing in a paper's title is ever considered a genuine integrity concern
option_c: Recycled text is judged solely by its word count, regardless of which section it appears in
option_d: COPE guidance applies exclusively to recycled data, never to recycled prose
option_e: Recycled text in a methods section is generally viewed as more acceptable than the same overlap in a discussion section
explanation_correct: COPE's position on text recycling notes that editors weigh several factors case by case, including where the overlap occurs in the paper; text recycled in a methods section is often more defensible, since procedures may legitimately be described in similar or identical language across an author's own studies, whereas the same degree of overlap in a discussion section is more likely to raise concerns about disguising a lack of original contribution.

question: A researcher removes participant names from a dataset but keeps a separate key linking each pseudonym back to the original identity, for potential re-contact later. Under GDPR, does this pseudonymized dataset fall outside the regulation's scope?
option_a: Yes, any dataset with names removed is automatically anonymized and therefore exempt from GDPR entirely
option_b: No, because GDPR does not recognize any distinction between pseudonymized and fully identifiable data
option_c: Yes, but only if the research is being conducted outside of the European Union
option_d: No, pseudonymized data still counts as personal data under GDPR since re-identification remains possible via the key
option_e: No, because Article 89 bans the use of pseudonymization in research altogether
explanation_correct: GDPR distinguishes pseudonymized data, where identity is masked but recoverable via a separate key, from truly anonymized data, where re-identification is not reasonably possible by any means. Pseudonymization is one of the safeguards the regulation encourages for research (Article 89), but pseudonymized data remains personal data and stays within GDPR's scope as long as a re-identification key exists anywhere; only genuinely anonymized data falls outside the regulation entirely.

question: Why does ICMJE require clinical trial registration to occur before participant enrollment begins, rather than simply requiring registration at some point before publication?
option_a: Registering before enrollment is required solely it speeds up the ethics review board's approval process
option_b: Registering before enrollment prevents researchers from selecting or changing outcomes after seeing how the results turn out
option_c: Registering before enrollment is required because unregistered trials are illegal to conduct in most countries
option_d: Registering before enrollment is required because participants are entitled to see the registration before consenting
option_e: Registering before enrollment has no real purpose beyond satisfying an arbitrary administrative deadline
explanation_correct: Clinical trial registration exists to prevent selective publication and selective outcome reporting. If registration happened only before publication rather than before enrollment, researchers could effectively choose their outcomes after seeing the data, then register a protocol that matches whichever results looked favorable. Requiring prospective registration, before the first participant is enrolled, closes that loophole by creating a public, timestamped record of the intended outcomes before anyone knows how the trial will turn out.

question: In the influential 2019 US National Academies framing, 'reproducibility' means:
option_a: Having your work cited by others
option_b: Publishing in a reproducible journal
option_c: Getting consistent results from a new study with newly collected data
option_d: Consistent results using the same data, code, and analysis steps
option_e: Repeating an experiment in a different country
explanation_correct: The National Academies define reproducibility as obtaining consistent results using the same input data, computational steps, methods, code, and conditions of analysis (computational reproducibility).

question: What is 'preregistration' of a study?
option_a: Submitting a completed manuscript to a journal before it has actually been written
option_b: Paying a required publication fee to the journal well in advance
option_c: Formally registering for and obtaining a personal ORCID iD
option_d: Publicly specifying hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or examining the data
option_e: Registering in advance to attend an upcoming academic conference
explanation_correct: Preregistration means documenting a study's hypotheses and planned analyses in a public registry before data are collected or analyzed, helping distinguish confirmatory from exploratory work.

question: In the 2019 National Academies distinction, 'replicability' refers to:
option_a: Consistent results across studies using newly collected data
option_b: Formally translating a published paper into a different language
option_c: Depositing and archiving a dataset within a trusted repository
option_d: Simply rerunning the exact same code on the exact same original dataset
option_e: Reformatting an already-published paper to submit to a new journal
explanation_correct: Replicability is obtaining consistent results across different studies that each answer the same scientific question with their own newly collected data, in contrast to reproducibility, which reuses the same data.

question: How does a Registered Report differ from ordinary preregistration?
option_a: The study protocol is peer reviewed before data collection and can receive 'in-principle acceptance'
option_b: It is generally reviewed by an editor after the study has been completed and submitted for publication
option_c: It functions mainly as a second, duplicate registration filed alongside a standard preregistration
option_d: It is a publishing format used mainly for randomized clinical trials rather than other study designs
option_e: It mainly involves registering a study's title and authors rather than its hypotheses or methods
explanation_correct: In a Registered Report, a Stage 1 manuscript (introduction and methods) is peer reviewed before data collection; if accepted in principle, the journal commits to publishing the completed study regardless of whether results are positive, reducing publication bias.

question: The TOP Guidelines, adopted by many journals, primarily address:
option_a: Setting standard limits on the article processing charges journals may bill
option_b: Transparency and openness standards for journal data and code policies
option_c: Defining the technical syntax used for persistent identifier strings
option_d: Producing an annual ranking of universities based on research output
option_e: Standardizing the copyright transfer terms used in publishing agreements
explanation_correct: The Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, from the Center for Open Science, give journals a menu of standards such as data, analysis code, and materials transparency, each implementable at increasing levels of stringency.

question: Which set of problems are Registered Reports specifically designed to reduce?
option_a: Peer reviewer shortages
option_b: Plagiarism and image duplication
option_c: Slow typesetting and high APCs
option_d: Bias, p-hacking, and HARKing
option_e: Data storage costs
explanation_correct: By fixing hypotheses and analyses before results are known and guaranteeing publication of sound studies, Registered Reports target publication bias, p-hacking (exploiting analytic flexibility), and HARKing.

question: In the TOP Guidelines, what does having 'three levels' for each standard mean?
option_a: It means that three completely separate journals must formally agree on a decision
option_b: It means the review process for a manuscript happens across three separate rounds
option_c: Each standard can be implemented with increasing stringency, from disclosure to verification
option_d: It means the TOP Guidelines contain only three standards in total
option_e: It means authors are given exactly three separate attempts to submit their manuscript
explanation_correct: Each TOP standard can be adopted at one of three levels of increasing rigor: Level 1 (Disclosed) — authors state whether the practice was followed; Level 2 (Shared and Cited) — the practice is carried out and the output cited; Level 3 (Certified) — an independent party certifies compliance. This lets journals adopt openness incrementally.

question: Why does the 2019 National Academies report argue that a lack of replicability is not always a sign of error or misconduct?
option_a: Non-replication can arise from real complexity and can itself drive discovery
option_b: Because academic journals, as a rule, never actually publish replication studies
option_c: Because every single instance of non-replication is ultimately caused by fraud
option_d: Because replicating a scientific study is considered impossible in principle
option_e: Because the terms replicability and reproducibility are, in fact, identical concepts
explanation_correct: The report notes that some non-replication is expected and even useful: it can result from the genuine complexity of systems under study and can prompt new hypotheses, so it should not be automatically equated with error or misconduct.

question: Which organization created and maintains the TOP Guidelines and the associated 'TOP Factor' concept?
option_a: UNESCO, through its open science division
option_b: The Center for Open Science (COS)
option_c: Crossref, as part of its metadata services
option_d: Elsevier, as a commercial publisher
option_e: Clarivate, through its Web of Science platform
explanation_correct: The Center for Open Science developed the TOP Guidelines (introduced in Science in 2015) and the TOP Factor, an alternative journal metric scoring journals on their transparency policies rather than citations.

question: What is a computational notebook (e.g., Jupyter, R Markdown, Quarto) useful for in reproducible research?
option_a: A secure place specifically designed for storing login passwords
option_b: Combining code, outputs, and narrative in one rerunnable document
option_c: A tool used specifically for ranking academic journals
option_d: A tool intended to entirely replace the formal peer-review process
option_e: A service used specifically for assigning persistent DOIs
explanation_correct: Computational notebooks interleave executable code, results (tables, figures), and prose, letting others follow and re-execute the exact analytical steps - supporting transparency and computational reproducibility.

question: Why is sharing analysis code alongside a paper important for reproducibility?
option_a: Sharing the code is thought to remove the need to share any underlying data
option_b: It lets others see how data were processed and rerun the analysis
option_c: Sharing the analysis code is believed to directly raise a journal's impact factor
option_d: Sharing the analysis code is a formal requirement for obtaining a DOI
option_e: Sharing the code mainly serves to make the resulting paper noticeably shorter
explanation_correct: Publishing the code makes the analytical steps transparent and allows independent verification and reuse; text descriptions of methods are often too incomplete to reproduce results without the actual code.

question: What is protocols.io used for?
option_a: A service used specifically for the long-term storage of research datasets
option_b: Creating and sharing detailed, versioned research protocols
option_c: A tool used specifically to rank published protocols by their citation count
option_d: A service used specifically for registering researchers' ORCID iDs
option_e: A tool used by publishers specifically to detect plagiarism in manuscripts
explanation_correct: protocols.io is a platform for authoring, sharing, and updating detailed research protocols (often with DOIs), improving methodological transparency and letting others reproduce procedures exactly.

question: What is the 'replication crisis' (or reproducibility crisis)?
option_a: A general shortage of academic journals willing to publish new research
option_b: A situation in which far too many replication studies are being published
option_c: A general and pervasive lack of citations across the scientific literature
option_d: A broader crisis concerning how research data is stored and archived
option_e: Many published results are difficult or impossible to reproduce
explanation_correct: The replication crisis refers to widespread difficulty reproducing or replicating published findings - notably highlighted in psychology and biomedicine - prompting reforms in transparency, preregistration, and statistics.

question: What is an 'electronic lab notebook' (ELN)?
option_a: A tablet device used casually for jotting down personal notes
option_b: A piece of software used specifically to manage bibliographic citations
option_c: Software for recording research activities, protocols, and data digitally
option_d: A specific type of preprint posted before formal peer review
option_e: A system used by journals specifically to manage manuscript submissions
explanation_correct: An ELN is digital software for documenting experiments, methods, and results, making records searchable, shareable, time-stamped, and easier to preserve and audit than paper lab notebooks - supporting reproducibility and integrity.

question: Why should a random 'seed' be set and reported in analyses involving randomness (e.g., simulations, machine learning)?
option_a: So that the underlying computational analysis simply runs faster overall
option_b: So that the resulting paper accumulates a higher number of citations
option_c: So that operations involving random numbers produce the same results every time
option_d: So that the final results of the analysis become fully encrypted
option_e: So that the resulting analysis can be formally assigned its own DOI
explanation_correct: Setting and reporting a random seed fixes the sequence of pseudo-random numbers, so a simulation, train/test split, or stochastic model yields identical results on re-execution - a small step that greatly aids computational reproducibility.

question: What are 'reporting guidelines' such as CONSORT (trials) and PRISMA (systematic reviews)?
option_a: Specialized software platforms used to manage the peer-review process
option_b: A formal set of rules governing how bibliographic references should be formatted
option_c: Systems used specifically for ranking academic journals against each other
option_d: Standardized legal frameworks that govern how research outputs may be licensed
option_e: Structured checklists specifying what information a study of a given type must report
explanation_correct: Reporting guidelines are checklists (e.g., CONSORT for randomized trials, PRISMA for systematic reviews, ARRIVE for animal studies) that define the minimum information needed for transparent, complete, and assessable reporting.

question: What is 'open materials' in the context of open methods?
option_a: Office supplies such as pens and paper that are provided completely free
option_b: Open access journal articles specifically, and nothing else
option_c: Making study materials like stimuli and protocols openly available for reuse
option_d: Textbooks that have entered the public domain and can be freely reused
option_e: Editorial pieces published openly by an academic journal
explanation_correct: Open materials means sharing the actual instruments and resources behind a study (surveys, stimuli, analysis code, protocols) so that others can scrutinize, reuse, and attempt to reproduce it - one of the components rewarded by Open Science Badges.

question: What is "The Turing Way"?
option_a: A ranking that orders universities according to their research output
option_b: A tool used specifically for indexing and tracking scholarly citations
option_c: A commercial software package used for performing statistical analysis
option_d: A server specifically dedicated to hosting early preprint manuscripts
option_e: An open handbook of good practices for reproducible research
explanation_correct: The Turing Way is an openly licensed, community-authored guide covering reproducible research, project design, communication, collaboration, and ethics, serving as a widely used reference for good practice.

question: What are 'Open Science Badges'?
option_a: Formal awards given specifically to a field's single most-cited paper each year
option_b: Formal certificates issued to individuals who serve as peer reviewers
option_c: Badges certifying that authors made data or materials openly available
option_d: Visual labels indicating that a journal has an unusually high impact factor
option_e: Name tags that identify attendees at academic conferences
explanation_correct: Open Science Badges (from the Center for Open Science) are earned incentives shown on articles indicating open data, open materials, or preregistration, nudging authors toward transparent practices.

question: Why is documenting the software versions and dependencies used in an analysis important?
option_a: Documenting this information is mainly a way to make the resulting files smaller
option_b: Because results can change with different software or package versions
option_c: Documenting this information is believed to directly increase citation counts
option_d: Documenting this information is a formal requirement for assigning a software license
option_e: Documenting software versions is considered relevant for physical computing hardware
explanation_correct: Analyses can produce different results under different versions of languages, packages, or libraries; capturing exact versions and dependencies (e.g., in an environment file) lets others rebuild the same environment and reproduce results.

question: What does 'preregistration' primarily help distinguish?
option_a: It primarily helps distinguish raw underlying data from analysis code
option_b: It primarily helps distinguish the paper's authors from its peer reviewers
option_c: It primarily helps distinguish open access publishing from subscription publishing
option_d: Confirmatory analyses planned in advance from exploratory ones
option_e: It primarily helps distinguish journals from institutional repositories
explanation_correct: By recording hypotheses and analysis plans before seeing the data, preregistration makes clear which analyses were planned (confirmatory) versus generated after looking at the data (exploratory), curbing practices like HARKing.

question: What is a 'container' (e.g., Docker) in the context of reproducible computation?
option_a: A physical box or crate used to store printed materials
option_b: A specific standardized format used for citing scholarly sources
option_c: A type of online service used specifically for storing research data
option_d: A specific category or type of academic journal
option_e: A packaged environment bundling code with its dependencies
explanation_correct: A container encapsulates an application together with its libraries and configuration, so the analysis behaves consistently across computers, greatly aiding reproducibility of complex computational workflows.

question: Why is publishing negative or null results valuable for reproducibility and the literature?
option_a: Because negative or null results are, as a general rule, always incorrect
option_b: Because studies with negative or null results simply cannot undergo peer review
option_c: Because publishing negative results is believed to raise a journal's impact factor
option_d: Because omitting them creates publication bias
option_e: Because publishing this kind of result is a formal requirement for obtaining a DOI
explanation_correct: When only positive findings are published, the literature overstates effects and wastes effort on already-failed approaches; publishing null/negative results counters publication bias and supports accurate meta-analysis and reproducibility.

question: What did the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (2015) find?
option_a: Psychology as a field showed strong reproducibility, with only a small number of studies affected
option_b: Most of the studies in the sample replicated closely, with similar effect sizes to the originals
option_c: The project concluded that replication studies are generally not a useful way to check findings
option_d: The project attributed most of the non-replications it found to fraud or misconduct by the original researchers
option_e: Many psychology studies did not reproduce when independently replicated
explanation_correct: The Open Science Collaboration's large-scale replication of 100 psychology studies found that a large share failed to replicate, with replicated effect sizes typically much smaller than the originals - a landmark empirical demonstration of the replication crisis.

question: What is 'p-hacking'?
option_a: The unethical practice of directly stealing p-values from other researchers' work
option_b: Selectively reporting analyses that reach statistical significance
option_c: The practice of formally registering a study's hypotheses before collecting data
option_d: The practice of openly sharing one's analysis code alongside a publication
option_e: The straightforward, correct statistical procedure for computing a p-value
explanation_correct: P-hacking exploits analytic flexibility - testing multiple specifications, adding/dropping cases, or trying many outcomes - and reporting only significant results, which produces spurious 'significant' findings and undermines reproducibility.

question: What is Binder (mybinder.org) used for?
option_a: A traditional bookbinding service used to physically bind printed journal articles
option_b: Turning a code repository into a live, interactive computing environment
option_c: A cloud service used specifically for the permanent, long-term storage of large datasets
option_d: A service used specifically for assigning persistent DOIs to shared code
option_e: A platform used specifically for ranking different pieces of research software
explanation_correct: Binder builds an executable environment from a repository's contents and dependency files, letting anyone run the notebooks interactively online - lowering the barrier to reproducing and exploring an analysis.

question: How does the 'garden of forking paths' concept relate to reproducibility problems?
option_a: It describes a particular kind of network built from citation relationships between papers
option_b: It describes a specific technical layout used for organizing stored data files
option_c: Undeclared analytic choices can lead to false positives without conscious p-hacking
option_d: It refers to a standardized template used when writing a study preregistration
option_e: It refers to a specific type of software container used in computing
explanation_correct: The 'garden of forking paths' (Gelman and Loken) notes that researcher degrees of freedom - defensible choices made contingent on the data - can inflate false positives even without intentional p-hacking, which is why preregistration of analysis plans matters.

question: Why is the American Statistical Association's guidance often summarized as 'a p-value is not a measure of effect size or importance'?
option_a: Because reporting an effect size alongside a p-value is technically illegal in most fields
option_b: Because p-values, understood correctly, are fundamentally wrong to compute
option_c: Because a p-value reflects evidence against a null, not the size or importance of an effect
option_d: Because a p-value is understood to directly and precisely measure a study's reproducibility
option_e: Because a p-value is, mathematically, exactly the same thing as a confidence interval
explanation_correct: The ASA statement warns against conflating statistical significance with importance: a p-value speaks to compatibility with a null model, not to how large or consequential an effect is, so reporting effect sizes and uncertainty is essential.

question: What is the difference between 'methods reproducibility' and 'results reproducibility' as sometimes distinguished in the literature?
option_a: Methods reproducibility is what some other terminologies (e.g. Claerbout's) call 'replicability' instead
option_b: Methods reproducibility is providing enough detail (code, data, protocols) to repeat the study exactly
option_c: Methods reproducibility applies only to computational or simulation studies, not experimental research more broadly
option_d: Results reproducibility can be fully established even if methods reproducibility is not satisfied
option_e: The distinction is mainly relevant to survey methodology, not experimental or computational science
explanation_correct: Goodman, Fanelli, and Ioannidis's lexicon distinguishes methods reproducibility (documenting procedures and data in enough detail to repeat them exactly) from results reproducibility (obtaining the same findings from an independent study with closely matched procedures); the former is what enables the latter to even be tested.

question: Why can proprietary or point-and-click software workflows hinder reproducibility compared with scripted analyses?
option_a: Using proprietary, point-and-click software for analysis is considered outright illegal
option_b: Scripted analyses are, in every single case, simply faster to run than GUI-based ones
option_c: Point-and-click software workflows are technically incapable of producing figures
option_d: Manual, GUI-based steps are hard to document exactly and repeat
option_e: Graphical software interfaces are what handle the technical process of assigning DOIs
explanation_correct: Clicking through menus (as in GUI-based image tools or spreadsheets) leaves no complete, shareable record of what was done, so others struggle to retrace or reproduce the steps; a script captures the full sequence of operations, which can be inspected and re-executed exactly.

question: What is the aim of workflow-management tools like Snakemake in reproducible research?
option_a: To produce a formal ranking that compares different analysis pipelines
option_b: To manage and coordinate the formal peer review of submitted manuscripts
option_c: To provide long-term, centralized storage for large research datasets
option_d: Automating multi-step analysis pipelines in a documented, rerunnable way
option_e: To handle the formal process of assigning open-source software licenses
explanation_correct: Workflow managers let researchers specify each processing step and its inputs/outputs so an entire pipeline can be reproduced, scaled, and rerun consistently across systems, with the workflow itself serving as documentation.

question: How does a Registered Report guard against publication bias differently from simply preregistering a study?
option_a: The study is peer reviewed and accepted in principle before results are known
option_b: The study protocol is reviewed by the journal only after data collection and analysis are complete
option_c: This publishing format works by guaranteeing in advance that the study's results will turn out positive
option_d: This particular publishing format is notable specifically for skipping the peer-review stage entirely
option_e: There is, in fact, no meaningful difference between this format and simple preregistration
explanation_correct: Preregistration records the plan but does not secure publication; a Registered Report adds pre-results peer review and in-principle acceptance, so outcome-independent publication is guaranteed, directly counteracting the file-drawer/publication-bias problem.

question: Why is 'open data plus closed code' often insufficient for computational reproducibility?
option_a: The underlying dataset is considered less important than the analysis code for reproducibility
option_b: Without the code, others can't know how data were transformed into the results
option_c: Because the analysis code is thought to functionally replace the need for the data itself
option_d: Because open data is a more recent requirement than open code, and journals haven't caught up yet
option_e: Because keeping the analysis code closed actually makes the overall computation run faster
explanation_correct: Reproducing computational results generally requires both the data and the exact processing steps; if the code is unavailable, the transformation from raw data to results is opaque and cannot be faithfully repeated.

question: Why did the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology report that many original cancer studies could not even be fully assessed, beyond questions of whether they replicated?
option_a: Because the original cancer studies in question were later found to be outright fraudulent
option_b: Original papers lacked methodological detail, and authors often couldn't share materials
option_c: Because the field of cancer biology is considered fundamentally unreproducible as a matter of principle
option_d: Because, in fact, every single one of the original studies included ended up replicating successfully
option_e: Because attempting to replicate a published study is considered illegal under research regulations
explanation_correct: A striking finding of the Cancer Biology project was that incomplete reporting and lack of access to protocols, reagents, and data made many studies impossible to reproduce as written - a transparency failure distinct from outright replication success or failure.

question: How do preregistration and Registered Reports specifically counter HARKing and the garden of forking paths?
option_a: Because using these approaches is believed to eliminate the need for any statistical analysis at all
option_b: Because adopting these approaches automatically and mechanically increases a study's sample size
option_c: Fixing hypotheses in advance prevents HARKing and undeclared analytic flexibility
option_d: Because using these approaches provides a guarantee that a finding will replicate
option_e: Because these particular safeguards are understood to work only within formal clinical trials
explanation_correct: Committing to hypotheses and analyses in advance means researchers cannot later reframe exploratory findings as predictions (HARKing) or exploit data-dependent choices among many paths, both of which otherwise drive spurious confirmatory results.

question: Why is a shared container image often considered stronger evidence of computational reproducibility than a dependency list alone?
option_a: Because containers are, by design, the mechanism used to formally assign persistent DOIs
option_b: Because a simple dependency list is technically incapable of ever being shared with others
option_c: Because sharing a plain dependency list is considered outright illegal under most licenses
option_d: A container captures the entire working environment as an executable artifact
option_e: Because a packaged container image is, in every case, simply smaller in file size than a list
explanation_correct: A dependency list may omit system-level libraries or resolve to different versions when rebuilt, whereas a container preserves the actual environment as a runnable artifact, making it more likely others obtain identical results.

question: What is the significance of 'many analysts, one dataset' studies for understanding reproducibility?
option_a: With enough independent analysts, the 'true' effect size can be triangulated by simply averaging their results
option_b: Independent teams analyzing the same data can reach different results from analytic choices
option_c: Once all teams are given identical data and instructions, their results reliably converge
option_d: Studies of this kind are, in essence, primarily concerned with how data should be physically stored
option_e: These findings are specific to sports analytics and don't generalize to other empirical fields
explanation_correct: In Silberzahn et al.'s landmark study, 29 teams of 61 analysts examined identical data on the same question (whether soccer referees show bias against dark-skin-toned players) and produced effect sizes ranging from 0.89 to 2.93 in odds-ratio units, with 69% finding a significant effect and 31% not. Neither analysts' prior beliefs, expertise, nor peer-rated quality explained the variation. As the authors put it, crowdsourcing data analysis "makes transparent how defensible, yet subjective, analytic choices influence research results," underscoring the value of preregistration, multiverse analysis, and transparency.

question: Why is documenting provenance and computational environment increasingly framed as part of making workflows 'FAIR'?
option_a: Because treating workflows as FAIR research objects lets others find, access, and rerun them, with provenance capturing the execution history needed for reuse
option_b: Because FAIR requires workflows to be made fully open access; provenance and environment details are recorded to satisfy that openness requirement
option_c: Because FAIR workflows are, by definition, also reproducible; satisfying the FAIR principles guarantees a workflow's results can be replicated
option_d: Because computational workflows are, by their very nature, fundamentally incapable of being shared
option_e: Because provenance and environment details are captured to assess workflow quality and correctness, which FAIR treats as a core principle alongside the four standard ones
explanation_correct: Extending FAIR to workflows (via the WCI-FW group's FAIR data and software adaptations) recognizes that reproducible science needs the pipelines themselves to be documented, shareable, and rerunnable; provenance falls under Reusability (R1.3), and computational environment details support Interoperability, since missing context is one of the main barriers to porting workflows across systems.

question: How does selective reporting of outcomes in clinical trials undermine reproducibility, and what mechanism addresses it?
option_a: Selective reporting of trial outcomes is generally understood to have no meaningful effect at all
option_b: The recommended mechanism for addressing this problem is to stop registering clinical trials altogether
option_c: Reporting only the most favorable outcomes actually tends to improve a study's overall reproducibility
option_d: Outcome-switching biases evidence; prospective trial registration lets others detect it
option_e: The recommended mechanism for addressing this problem is simply to publish trial results faster
explanation_correct: When trialists emphasize outcomes that turned out significant and drop pre-specified ones, results are biased and hard to reproduce; mandatory prospective registration of primary outcomes enables comparison of what was planned versus reported, deterring outcome-switching.

question: Why is 'reproducible' not the same as 'correct'?
option_a: An analysis can be reproducible only if it has also been independently peer-reviewed and validated
option_b: An analysis can be reproducible yet still be based on flawed data or wrong assumptions
option_c: A reproducible analysis is generally understood to also be a correct one
option_d: A correct analysis is generally understood to also be a reproducible one
option_e: Neither of these two properties is considered relevant when evaluating research
explanation_correct: Reproducibility ensures the reported results follow from the stated data and code, enabling scrutiny; but it says nothing about whether the data are sound or the methods appropriate, so a reproducible result can still be wrong.

question: Why do some scholars argue that a degree of non-replication is a normal and even healthy feature of science rather than a pure 'crisis'?
option_a: Because non-replication is thought to result mainly from journals declining to publish replication studies in the first place
option_b: Because these scholars hold that non-replication is always the result of researchers making outright errors
option_c: Because these scholars believe science should generally avoid drawing attention to its own mistakes
option_d: Because a degree of self-correction is normal, but these scholars argue science should not actively pursue it
option_e: Variability in complex systems means some non-replication is expected and can inform discovery
explanation_correct: As the National Academies noted, some non-replication legitimately arises from the complexity and stochasticity of what is studied and can drive discovery; the crisis framing is better aimed at the avoidable causes - bias, questionable practices, and inadequate transparency - than at all non-replication.

question: How does the incentive structure of academic publishing contribute to the reproducibility crisis, and what reforms target this?
option_a: Publishing incentives mainly affect how quickly papers appear in print, not whether their results hold up
option_b: The proposed solution is simply to place even greater editorial emphasis on producing novel findings
option_c: A preference for novel results over replications discourages verification; reforms reward rigor instead
option_d: The reforms scholars propose mainly involve counting replication attempts the same way citations are currently counted, with no other changes needed
option_e: Because researchers are personally responsible for the crisis, incentive structures are considered a separate, unrelated issue
explanation_correct: Because journals and evaluators have favored striking positive findings, researchers are pushed toward practices that reduce reproducibility and away from replication; structural fixes - outcome-independent publishing, registered replications, transparency mandates, and reforming what counts in assessment - realign incentives with reliability.

question: What is a 'multiverse analysis', and how does it improve transparency about analytic flexibility?
option_a: A technique in which every result except the single best-looking one is simply deleted
option_b: An approach in which a single analysis is run once and its result is simply reported as-is
option_c: A speculative technique that involves analyzing data collected from parallel universes
option_d: Reporting how results vary across reasonable analytic choices
option_e: A specific technical term referring to a type of software container used in computing
explanation_correct: A multiverse (or specification-curve) analysis runs and reports the outcome across the full set of defensible analytic choices, making the dependence of conclusions on those choices explicit rather than hidden - directly countering selective reporting and the garden of forking paths.

question: Why can strict computational reproducibility still fail over long timescales, even with shared code and data?
option_a: Long-term computational reproducibility, in practice, essentially never fails once code is shared
option_b: Software ecosystems evolve, so shared code can stop running as languages, libraries, or platforms change
option_c: Because attempting to reproduce results is considered legally prohibited after just one year
option_d: Because the underlying data involved is understood to simply disappear instantly over time
option_e: Because academic journals, as a matter of policy, routinely delete the code they receive
explanation_correct: Even well-shared analyses can stop running years later as languages, libraries, and platforms change or vanish — a phenomenon sometimes called "code rot" or "dependency rot." Strategies like containerizing and archiving the full environment, preferring open and stable formats, and emulation can help preserve executability, though none is a permanent guarantee.

question: Besides sharing data and code, why do researchers also need to document the computational environment (e.g., software versions and dependencies) used in an analysis?
option_a: Because the same code can produce different results when run with different software versions or dependencies
option_b: Because documenting the environment is a formal requirement for assigning a dataset's DOI
option_c: Because listing software versions is understood to automatically improve a paper's citation count
option_d: Because the computational environment is thought to functionally replace the need for sharing code
option_e: Because documenting the environment is mainly a courtesy to reviewers, with no bearing on reproducibility itself
explanation_correct: Code that runs correctly in one environment can produce different results (or fail entirely) in another due to differences in software versions, libraries, or operating systems; documenting the environment lets others recreate the exact conditions needed to reproduce results.

question: What is the value of preregistering analysis plans in observational (non-experimental) studies?
option_a: Preregistering an observational study's analysis plan is thought to replace formal peer review
option_b: Preregistration, as a practice, is understood to be useful for true experimental studies
option_c: Preregistering an analysis plan is believed to guarantee that any resulting conclusions are causal
option_d: Preregistering an analysis plan is thought to remove the need to actually collect data
option_e: It constrains analytic flexibility, distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analyses
explanation_correct: Even without an experiment, observational analyses face many analytic choices; preregistering the plan separates confirmatory from exploratory analyses and curbs the selective, data-dependent decisions that inflate false positives.

question: A researcher takes a published study's original code and original dataset, runs the analysis again, and gets the same numbers. What has she just done?
option_a: Reproduced the result
option_b: Replicated the result
option_c: Falsified the result
option_d: Preregistered the result
option_e: Peer-reviewed the result
explanation_correct: Rerunning the same analysis on the same data to confirm the same result is reproducing (in the common NASEM framing). Replicating would instead mean collecting new data to see if the finding holds again.

question: Why can publication bias distort systematic reviews and meta-analyses?
option_a: Because systematic reviews, by their nature, simply ignore every individual study available
option_b: Because researchers conducting meta-analyses are known to routinely fabricate their underlying data
option_c: Positive-result studies are more likely to be published, so reviews overestimate effects
option_d: Because studies that report null or negative results are generally found to be incorrect
option_e: Because systematic reviews of this kind draw their evidence exclusively from preprint servers
explanation_correct: If positive findings are preferentially published, a meta-analysis built on the visible literature will over-represent positive effects and overstate the true effect, which is why registries and searching for unpublished results matter.

question: Why is 'reproducible but not replicable' a coherent and informative outcome?
option_a: This outcome would specifically indicate that the original analysis had been fraudulently conducted
option_b: This particular combination of outcomes is, on its face, a logical contradiction
option_c: A result can be computationally reproducible yet fail to replicate with fresh data
option_d: This outcome would specifically mean that the underlying dataset had since been deleted
option_e: It would simply mean that the two terms, reproducible and replicable, are actually synonyms
explanation_correct: Because reproducibility and replicability are distinct, a study can be perfectly reproducible while a fresh-data replication does not reproduce the effect, pointing to generalizability or robustness issues rather than a mistake in the original computation.

question: Crossref is best described as:
option_a: A government agency responsible for regulating scholarly publishing
option_b: A university ranking service that compares institutions annually
option_c: A social networking platform designed specifically for scientists
option_d: A nonprofit that registers DOIs and metadata for scholarly content
option_e: A commercial publisher that produces its own line of academic journals
explanation_correct: Crossref is a not-for-profit membership organization, founded in 2000, that registers DOIs and rich metadata for journal articles, books, and other scholarly outputs, and offers services to find, cite, and link them.

question: OpenAlex is:
option_a: A preprint server where researchers post manuscripts before formal review
option_b: A free and open index of scholarly works, authors, institutions, sources, and more
option_c: A commercial database like Web of Science with subscription-only access
option_d: A reference manager used to organize and format bibliographic citations
option_e: A tool used by publishers specifically to detect plagiarism
explanation_correct: OpenAlex, run by the nonprofit OurResearch, is a free, openly licensed (CC0) index of scholarly entities: works, authors, sources, institutions, topics, publishers, and funders, offered with a free API.

question: What does the Unpaywall service help users do?
option_a: A service that ranks academic journals by their overall prestige
option_b: A tool that helps users bypass all forms of copyright restriction
option_c: A cloud service that lets researchers store their own personal data
option_d: A payment platform used specifically to pay article processing charges
option_e: Find legal, freely available open access versions of scholarly articles
explanation_correct: Unpaywall, from OurResearch, locates legally available open access copies of articles by harvesting repositories and publisher sites, delivered via a browser extension and API.

question: What is the primary difference in scope between Crossref and DataCite?
option_a: Crossref focuses mainly on registering DOIs for publications like journal articles
option_b: DataCite is, in fact, a commercial publisher that sells subscriptions
option_c: Crossref primarily handles research data while DataCite handles journal articles
option_d: Neither Crossref nor DataCite actually issues any DOIs at all
option_e: Crossref and DataCite are, in fact, simply the same organization
explanation_correct: Both are DOI Registration Agencies licensed by the International DOI Foundation, but they specialize by content type

question: What does SPARC (in the scholarly-communications context) stand for and do?
option_a: SPARC: advocates for open access, open data, and open education
option_b: A commercial publisher that sells subscriptions to its own journals
option_c: A commercial metrics firm that sells citation and impact data
option_d: A data repository whose main function is storing research datasets
option_e: A commercial ranking agency that produces annual university rankings
explanation_correct: SPARC is the Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition, a nonprofit whose members are libraries and academic organizations, advocating for open access, open data, and open education and driving policy change.

question: The Principles of Open Scholarly Infrastructure (POSI) are organized around which three areas?
option_a: Scalability, security, and profitability
option_b: Peer review, editing, and typesetting
option_c: Transparency, accountability, and compliance
option_d: Findability, accessibility, and reuse
option_e: Governance, sustainability, and insurance
explanation_correct: POSI groups its principles into governance (e.g., stakeholder-governed, cannot lobby), sustainability (e.g., transparent operations, revenue from services not data), and insurance (e.g., open source, data available for others to replicate if the organization fails).

question: Which organization is chiefly known for research, advocacy, and tools (such as 'Infra Finder') to help sustain and fund open scholarly infrastructure?
option_a: arXiv, a preprint server for physics and math
option_b: Elsevier, a large commercial publisher
option_c: Clarivate, a commercial analytics company
option_d: ORCID, a researcher identifier registry
option_e: Invest in Open Infrastructure (IOI)
explanation_correct: Invest in Open Infrastructure (IOI) is an independent nonprofit that produces research, advisory work, and tools like Infra Finder to help the community understand, coordinate investment in, and sustain open research infrastructure.

question: FORCE11 is best known as the community associated with which of the following?
option_a: The Budapest Open Access Initiative, an early open access declaration
option_b: The Handle System, the technology underlying DOI resolution
option_c: The FAIR Data Principles, a framework for research data reuse
option_d: The Journal Impact Factor, a widely used citation metric
option_e: The h-index, a common measure of researcher productivity
explanation_correct: FORCE11 (Future of Research Communications and e-Scholarship) is a community that helped produce foundational frameworks including the FAIR guiding principles, the Joint Declaration of Data Citation Principles, and the Software Citation Principles.

question: POSI's Sustainability principles state that revenue should be generated "from services, not data." What is the reasoning behind this distinction?
option_a: Data related to running the infrastructure should remain community property, so revenue instead comes from things like value-added services, consulting, or membership fees
option_b: Selling data is explicitly required, since it is the only sustainable revenue source available to nonprofit infrastructure
option_c: POSI considers all forms of revenue generation equally acceptable, with no distinction between data and services
option_d: Membership fees and consulting are prohibited under POSI, leaving data sales as the only compliant option
option_e: The distinction applies only to for-profit infrastructure providers, not to nonprofits
explanation_correct: POSI's Sustainability principles state that data related to running scholarly infrastructure should be treated as community property, not a revenue source. Instead, appropriate revenue comes from value-added services, consulting, API Service Level Agreements, or membership fees, revenue tied to what the organization does, not what it holds.

question: What is the main purpose of digital preservation services like CLOCKSS?
option_a: To handle the technical process of assigning DOIs to journal content
option_b: To calculate and publish official journal impact factor scores
option_c: To ensure scholarly content remains accessible in the long term
option_d: To scan published content and detect instances of plagiarism
option_e: To produce an annual ranking of academic journals by prestige
explanation_correct: CLOCKSS is a "dark archive" that preserves scholarly content but keeps it inaccessible until a "trigger event" occurs (e.g., a publisher ceasing operations), at which point the content becomes freely available to everyone.

question: What does OpenAIRE do?
option_a: Sells discounted airline tickets specifically to traveling researchers
option_b: Handles the technical process of assigning ORCID iDs to researchers
option_c: Directly publishes its own line of peer-reviewed academic journals
option_d: Provides open infrastructure to support open science across Europe
option_e: Produces an annual ranking of European universities by research output
explanation_correct: OpenAIRE is a European-rooted nonprofit infrastructure that aggregates metadata on research outputs, supports open-science policy and practice, and offers services connecting publications, data, software, and funding across a network of national hubs.

question: What is the Public Knowledge Project (PKP) best known for?
option_a: A commercial citation database sold on a subscription basis
option_b: A government funding agency that distributes competitive research grants
option_c: Developing free, open-source software such as Open Journal Systems
option_d: A commercial firm that produces annual university rankings
option_e: A preprint server where researchers post manuscripts before review
explanation_correct: PKP develops open-source publishing software, most prominently Open Journal Systems (OJS), which powers thousands of journals worldwide, especially supporting low-cost and diamond open-access publishing.

question: What is COAR (the Confederation of Open Access Repositories)?
option_a: A single, centralized global repository that hosts all open access content
option_b: A commercial vendor that sells repository software to institutions
option_c: An association that helps align open-access repositories worldwide
option_d: A citation index used to track how often research outputs are referenced
option_e: A funding body that distributes grants for repository development
explanation_correct: COAR is a global, member-based association that promotes and coordinates repositories - developing interoperability, shared practices, and initiatives like COAR Notify - to strengthen the worldwide network of open-access repositories.

question: What service does BASE (Bielefeld Academic Search Engine) provide?
option_a: A search engine indexing metadata of open documents worldwide
option_b: A formal peer-review service offered directly to academic journals
option_c: A commercial platform for selling discounted academic books
option_d: A service that produces formal rankings of individual researchers
option_e: A registration agency that handles the technical process of assigning DOIs
explanation_correct: BASE, run by Bielefeld University Library, is one of the largest search engines for open-access and repository content, harvesting metadata from thousands of sources to help users discover scholarly documents.

question: What is CORE (core.ac.uk) known for?
option_a: An annual ranking service that ranks universities by research output
option_b: A commercial platform that sells journal subscription packages
option_c: A repository that hosts only research datasets
option_d: A registry that handles the technical process of assigning ORCID iDs
option_e: Aggregating access to millions of open-access research papers
explanation_correct: CORE aggregates open-access full-text research papers from repositories and journals worldwide, offering search, text, and data-mining services and APIs over one of the largest collections of OA content.

question: What is the Center for Open Science (COS)?
option_a: A commercial citation database sold to libraries on subscription
option_b: A government funding agency that distributes competitive research grants
option_c: A nonprofit whose mission is to increase openness, integrity, and trustworthiness of research, and that builds the Open Science Framework (OSF)
option_d: A commercial firm that produces an annual ranking of universities
option_e: A subscription-based academic journal covering open science topics
explanation_correct: COS is a nonprofit that builds the Open Science Framework (a free project-management and sharing platform) and drives open-science initiatives including preregistration, Registered Reports, Open Science Badges, and the TOP Guidelines.

question: What is the Open Science Framework (OSF)?
option_a: A traditional peer-reviewed journal that publishes original research articles
option_b: A free platform to manage, share, and preregister research projects
option_c: A specific citation metric used to measure a researcher's overall impact
option_d: A government funding scheme that distributes competitive research grants
option_e: A commercial cloud storage platform available exclusively to private industry
explanation_correct: The OSF, from the Center for Open Science, is a free web platform supporting the whole research workflow - organizing projects, connecting storage and tools, sharing outputs, and preregistering studies - to promote transparency and collaboration.

question: What kind of organization is DataCite?
option_a: A commercial publisher that sells subscriptions to its own journal titles
option_b: A nonprofit DOI registration agency for research data and software
option_c: A commercial agency that produces annual rankings of research institutions
option_d: A social networking platform designed specifically for academic researchers
option_e: A government council that distributes competitive research funding grants
explanation_correct: DataCite is a nonprofit membership organization and DOI registration agency focused on making research data and other outputs citable and findable through DOIs and rich metadata, and it co-operates services like ROR.

question: Why are Crossref, DataCite, and ORCID sometimes described as key 'open' infrastructure organizations?
option_a: Because all three organizations are directly owned and operated by national governments
option_b: Because each organization sells exclusive access to its underlying data for profit
option_c: Because they are community-governed nonprofits many systems depend on
option_d: Because their primary function is to produce formal rankings of academic journals
option_e: Because each of the three organizations only serves researchers in a single country
explanation_correct: Crossref (publication DOIs/metadata), DataCite (data DOIs/metadata), and ORCID (researcher IDs) are member-governed nonprofits whose open identifiers and metadata underpin much of the scholarly ecosystem, exemplifying open scholarly infrastructure.

question: What does a 'dark archive' (e.g., CLOCKSS) mean?
option_a: An unofficial website that hosts pirated copies of copyrighted journal articles
option_b: An archive that specifically collects and stores books that have been formally banned
option_c: An archive released to the public only if the source becomes unavailable
option_d: An archive that preserves raw files but stores no descriptive metadata
option_e: A secret database maintained and operated exclusively by a national government
explanation_correct: A dark archive stores content securely without providing routine access; it makes material openly available only when a 'trigger event' (like a publisher ceasing operations) permanently removes the original, safeguarding continuity of access.

question: What is Crossref's 'Similarity Check' service used for?
option_a: A tool used specifically to detect and flag duplicate DOI registrations
option_b: Helping publishers screen manuscripts for plagiarism using iThenticate
option_c: A tool used specifically for comparing journals' official impact factors
option_d: A tool used specifically to match submitted manuscripts with suitable reviewers
option_e: A tool used specifically to check for similarity between different authors' names
explanation_correct: Similarity Check gives Crossref member publishers access to iThenticate to compare submissions against a large database of published content, supporting plagiarism screening during editorial evaluation.

question: What is OpenDOAR?
option_a: A curated global directory of open-access repositories and their policies
option_b: A platform that coordinates and manages the formal peer-review process
option_c: A registration agency responsible for issuing new DOIs to publishers
option_d: A formal technical standard governing the manufacturing of doors
option_e: A database that tracks funding awards made by research grant agencies
explanation_correct: OpenDOAR is an authoritative, curated directory of open-access repositories worldwide, listing their content types, policies, and features to help users and services find and assess repositories.

question: What is the role of the ISSN International Centre?
option_a: To handle the technical process of assigning DOIs to journal articles
option_b: To provide long-term hosting and storage for research datasets
option_c: To produce an annual ranking of journals by their overall prestige
option_d: To coordinate the ISSN network and assign ISSNs to serials
option_e: To handle the technical process of registering new ORCID iDs
explanation_correct: The ISSN International Centre, with a network of national centres, manages the assignment and registry of ISSNs - the standard identifiers for serial publications - ensuring serials can be reliably identified worldwide.

question: What does Crossref's 'Crossmark' feature provide to readers?
option_a: A numerical score indicating the likelihood that the article was plagiarized
option_b: The official journal impact factor of the publication in question
option_c: The corresponding author's registered ORCID iD, displayed for readers
option_d: A running total of how many times the article has been formally cited
option_e: A logo showing whether a document is current or has been updated
explanation_correct: Crossmark gives readers a way to check a document's status - confirming it is up to date and revealing publisher updates like corrections or retractions - helping ensure they are relying on the current, trustworthy version.

question: What is SCOSS (the Global Sustainability Coalition for Open Science Services)?
option_a: A single, centralized repository that hosts open-science content directly
option_b: A specific citation metric used to measure a service's overall impact
option_c: A commercial funder that provides grants to for-profit publishing companies
option_d: An initiative that coordinates community funding for open infrastructure
option_e: A ranking system that compares different open-science services to each other
explanation_correct: SCOSS runs a coordinated process to select vital open infrastructures (e.g., DOAJ, SHERPA, OpenCitations) and mobilize collective financial support from the community, addressing the sustainability of shared open services.

question: What is the 'Keepers Registry' used to check?
option_a: Which archiving agencies happen to charge a fee for their preservation services
option_b: Which academic journals currently have the highest official impact factor
option_c: Which individual authors keep their personal ORCID records fully updated
option_d: Which archiving agencies are preserving which continuing (serial) resources
option_e: Which specific DOIs have mistakenly been registered more than once
explanation_correct: The Keepers Registry monitors the archiving activity of participating preservation services, showing which serials/e-journals are being 'kept' and helping the community spot content at risk of loss - supporting collective preservation.

question: How does a platform like DSpace relate to institutional repositories?
option_a: A commercial system used specifically to rank institutional repositories
option_b: A commercial database used specifically to track scholarly citations
option_c: A preprint server used specifically for posting early manuscripts
option_d: A government funding agency that supports repository development
option_e: An open-source software platform used to build institutional repositories
explanation_correct: DSpace, stewarded by Lyrasis, is one of the most widely used open-source platforms on which institutions build repositories to store, manage, and provide open access to their outputs. Over 3,000 organizations currently use DSpace, most commonly research libraries running it as their institutional repository.

question: What distinguishes OpenAlex from proprietary databases like Scopus and Web of Science in the scholarly-information landscape?
option_a: OpenAlex is more expensive to access than either alternative
option_b: OpenAlex is a resource that covers research from biomedical discipline
option_c: OpenAlex is a resource that is directly owned and operated by US national government
option_d: OpenAlex is an index that only has abstract, it does not include any citation data
option_e: OpenAlex provides an openly licensed (CC0), free index of works, authors, institutions, sources, and more with an open API
explanation_correct: OpenAlex (by the nonprofit OurResearch) is a fully open catalog offering free, CC0-licensed data on works, authors, institutions, sources, topics, publishers, and funders, accessible via a free API. OpenAlex explicitly positions itself as an open replacement for paywalled services like Scopus and Web of Science, citing broader coverage, openness, and accessibility as its key advantages.

question: What is the significance of Crossref acquiring and openly releasing the Retraction Watch database (2023) for scholarly infrastructure?
option_a: It integrated a comprehensive, curated retraction dataset into open infrastructure (the Crossref API)
option_b: It made the underlying retraction data considerably more proprietary and restricted
option_c: It resulted in a formal ranking of journals based on their retraction counts
option_d: It led to previously retracted papers being permanently deleted from record
option_e: It effectively replaced the need for any form of formal peer review
explanation_correct: By acquiring the Retraction Watch database and making it openly available through its API, Crossref embedded a key integrity dataset into open scholarly infrastructure, enabling widespread, free reuse in discovery and integrity tools.

question: What role does Wikidata increasingly play in open scholarly infrastructure?
option_a: It is expected to eventually replace academic journals as the primary venue for publishing
option_b: It provides an open, linked knowledge base connecting scholarly entities
option_c: It primarily functions as a service that produces formal rankings of universities
option_d: Its main role is to handle the technical process of assigning new DOIs
option_e: Its main role is to host the complete full text of published articles
explanation_correct: Wikidata is an open, linked knowledge base connecting scholarly entities, researchers, institutions, publications, and their identifiers, through a web of interlinked data. As a "data hub," it forms part of the technical foundation for Open Science, letting information specialists and researchers link and enrich records (e.g., linking to ISSN, ORCID, and other identifier systems) without going through traditional publishing workflows.

question: Why is repository interoperability (e.g., shared metadata formats and protocols like OAI-PMH, or newer approaches like COAR Notify) important?
option_a: It mainly serves to increase the total physical storage capacity that repositories require
option_b: It is mainly a mechanism used to calculate and assign official impact factor scores
option_c: It is mainly used to produce a formal ranking that compares different repositories
option_d: It lets repositories, aggregators, and services exchange metadata and notifications consistently
option_e: It works primarily by encrypting the content stored within participating repositories
explanation_correct: OAI-PMH (the Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting) is a low-barrier mechanism that lets repositories act as "data providers," exposing structured metadata that aggregators and other services can harvest and build on. Newer protocols like COAR Notify extend this further, letting repositories exchange event notifications with external services such as peer review platforms. Together, these shared protocols connect distributed repositories into a functioning network rather than leaving them as isolated silos.

question: What is the difference in preservation approach between LOCKSS and a 'trigger'-based archive like Portico?
option_a: LOCKSS distributes many copies across libraries; Portico is centralized
option_b: There is, in practice, no meaningful difference between the two approaches
option_c: LOCKSS functions mainly as a service that produces formal rankings of journals
option_d: Portico, unlike LOCKSS, only preserves research datasets
option_e: Both LOCKSS and Portico store content in the cloud, with no physical library involvement
explanation_correct: LOCKSS ("Lots Of Copies Keep Stuff Safe") uses a decentralized, peer-to-peer model: member libraries each run a LOCKSS system that ingests and holds its own copy of content, and these systems continually compare copies with each other to detect and repair damage or loss. Portico, by contrast, operates as a centralized archive that releases content to participating libraries only when a defined "trigger event" occurs. These represent two complementary approaches to long-term e-journal preservation.

question: What does the Directory of Open Access Repositories ecosystem (OpenDOAR, re3data) collectively help users and services do?
option_a: It primarily helps produce formal rankings that compare individual researchers
option_b: It primarily handles the technical process of assigning new DOIs to outputs
option_c: It primarily functions as a tool for detecting plagiarism in submitted work
option_d: It primarily helps users find and compare repositories by discipline and content type
option_e: It primarily functions as a service for calculating official impact factor scores
explanation_correct: re3data and OpenDOAR are complementary registries that let researchers, funders, and systems locate and evaluate appropriate repositories, re3data for research data repositories (searchable by certification, metadata standards, and discipline), and OpenDOAR for open-access publication repositories. Both help match users and services with repositories that fit their needs.

question: Why is the sustainability of open scholarly infrastructure considered a systemic concern rather than a set of isolated organizational problems?
option_a: Because each open infrastructure operates independently, so a funding failure at one is unlikely to affect other services
option_b: Because open infrastructure services are typically funded by a stable, long-term government endowment
option_c: Because open infrastructure services are deeply interdependent, so a funding failure at one widely-relied-upon service can cascade and threaten the reliability of everything built on top of it
option_d: Because sustainability is mainly a branding concern, with little practical effect on whether a service keeps running
option_e: Because commercial infrastructure providers are generally expected to absorb open infrastructure services that fail
explanation_correct: Open infrastructure is rarely a single, standalone tool, identifiers resolve against registries, metadata flows between systems, and services build on one another. A funding shortfall or collapse at one widely-used piece of this network doesn't stay contained; it can cascade and threaten everything that depends on it. Landscape analyses have found some of the most heavily used open infrastructure services run with a core team of just two to five people, and that many would close within six months without continued grant funding, illustrating how thin and precarious this shared foundation really is.

question: Under POSI's Insurance principles, what does "patent non-assertion" actually require of an open infrastructure organization?
option_a: The organization is barred from obtaining any patents under any circumstances
option_b: It may hold patents to protect its own operations, but cannot use them to block the community from replicating the infrastructure
option_c: The organization must eventually transfer all existing patents to a national government upon request
option_d: t must license any patents it holds exclusively to a commercial partner
option_e: Patents are irrelevant to POSI, since the principles only address software licensing
explanation_correct: POSI's patent non-assertion principle doesn't forbid an organization from holding patents, it may still obtain them to protect its own operations. What it prohibits is using those patents to prevent the community from forking or replicating the infrastructure if needed, preserving the "insurance" that open source and open data are meant to provide.

question: Why does Crossref's Grant Linking System matter for the broader research-information graph?
option_a: It helps produce a formal ranking that compares different funders
option_b: It lets grants and funders be identified with persistent identifiers and linked to outputs
option_c: It is used to determine the specific article processing charges journals bill
option_d: It is used to entirely replace the traditional peer-review process
option_e: It helps in the anonymization process of a paper's listed authors
explanation_correct: By assigning persistent identifiers to grants through the Grant Linking System, and by standardizing funder identification, historically through the Open Funder Registry and increasingly through ROR (which Crossref, DataCite, and the California Digital Library jointly operate, and to which Crossref is migrating away from its own Funder Registry), Crossref enables outputs to be linked back to specific awards and funders in machine-readable ways. This strengthens the connected metadata graph used for reporting, compliance, and analysis.

question: What tension does the reliance on commercial platforms (e.g., for citation data, repositories, or workflow tools) create for the open-research movement?
option_a: Open, community-governed alternatives to these commercial platforms rarely exist
option_b: Dependence on proprietary services can create lock-in and access risks
option_c: Relying on these commercial platforms is generally the cheaper long-term option
option_d: There is, in practice, no meaningful tension created by this kind of commercial dependence
option_e: These commercial platforms are, in fact, already governed collectively by their user community
explanation_correct: When core research-information functions run on closed commercial platforms, for example, citation databases like Web of Science and Scopus, the community faces lock-in, non-transparent methodologies, and restricted access behind paywalls. Decisions about researchers' careers and institutions increasingly depend on these "black-box" indicators, which sit uneasily with open-science aims and put academic accountability and independence at risk. This is a key reason movements like the Barcelona Declaration support open, community-governed research information infrastructure.

question: How does the 'Metadata 2020' style push for richer, open metadata connect to the value of scholarly infrastructure?
option_a: It works mainly by restricting metadata records to paying subscribers
option_b: It's designed primarily around the needs of publishers
option_c: It reduces how much persistent identifiers matter, since metadata can stand in for them
option_d: It functions mainly as a certification system that scores and ranks organizations by metadata quality
option_e: Better, more open metadata increases discoverability across the ecosystem
explanation_correct: Metadata 2020 was a cross-community collaboration (publishers, librarians, funders, repositories, and researchers) built on the recognition that without complete, open, connected, and interoperable metadata, discoverability, use, and reuse are all held back, poor metadata limits what any downstream service, from search to analytics to funder reporting, can actually do with a research output.

question: Why is preservation infrastructure (dark archives, distributed preservation, the Keepers Registry) essential even when content is 'openly available' online?
option_a: Because content that is openly available online is understood to never disappear
option_b: Because open availability today does not guarantee long-term survival
option_c: Because preservation infrastructure of this kind mainly functions to rank competing journals
option_d: Because openly available content is assumed to be automatically archived by default
option_e: Because formal preservation infrastructure is considered relevant only for physical paper records
explanation_correct: A 2021 empirical study found 174 open-access journals had vanished from the web entirely between 2000 and 2019, demonstrating that being openly available online is not the same as being preserved. Without deliberate, monitored preservation, infrastructure like dark archives, distributed preservation networks, and the Keepers Registry, openly available works can still be permanently lost when hosts fail, funding runs out, or a publisher simply disappears.

question: Why is the distinction between 'open infrastructure' and merely 'free-to-use' services important when evaluating sustainability and independence?
option_a: Their main significance lies in how they help produce formal rankings of competing journals
option_b: In practice, platforms of this kind mainly end up benefiting only large commercial publishers
option_c: Adopting platforms of this kind generally requires purchasing expensive commercial software licenses
option_d: By providing free, community-supported software to run journals, they lower the cost barrier to publishing
option_e: Somewhat paradoxically, platforms of this kind actually work to prevent open access publishing
explanation_correct: Free and open-source publishing software like OJS substantially reduces the technical and financial barriers to running a journal. OJS alone is the world's most widely used journal management and publishing software, with adoption spanning every region globally, empowering universities, societies, and communities, notably in under-resourced regions, to operate no-fee diamond OA journals independently of commercial platforms. Platforms like Janeway serve a similar role for their own communities of adopters.

question: POSI's "Transparent Governance" principle specifically requires openness about which aspect of an infrastructure organization?
option_a: The organization's detailed financials, fees, and product roadmaps
option_b: The processes and policies for governing the organization and selecting its representatives
option_c: The source code and technical architecture of its software
option_d: The personal contact details of every individual staff member
option_e: The organization's negotiations with commercial vendors
explanation_correct: POSI's Transparent Governance principle specifically calls for openness about how the organization is governed, its decision-making processes and how representatives to governance groups are selected, so the community can trust that the organization is accountable to it. This is distinct from POSI's separate "Transparent Operations" principle under Sustainability, which covers financial and operational disclosure instead.

question: Why is the distinction between 'open infrastructure' and merely 'free-to-use' services important when evaluating sustainability and independence?
option_a: There is, in every meaningful respect, no real distinction between these two categories at all
option_b: A service can be free to use yet closed, single-vendor-controlled, or dependent on data lock-in
option_c: Being free to use is, by definition, always sufficient on its own to qualify a service as open
